BREAKING: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared a national energy emergency on March 24 2026, effective for one year. The Philippines has 53 days of gasoline, 46 days of diesel, and 39 days of jet fuel remaining. Gasoline prices have risen 35 to 45 percent in a single week. The government has shifted to a four-day workweek to conserve fuel. Flights may be grounded. The country is switching to dirtier Euro-II fuel standards because cleaner fuel is no longer available in sufficient quantities. People in Manila are walking to work.

The Philippines does not produce meaningful quantities of oil. It imports over 90 percent of its crude from the Gulf. The pipeline runs from the Persian Gulf, through the Strait of Hormuz, across the Indian Ocean, through the Malacca Strait, and into Philippine refineries. Every link in that chain is now under stress. The Hormuz gate has collapsed traffic 70 to 80 percent. The IRGC’s permissioned toll system accepts yuan and USDT, not dollars. The tankers that do transit carry cargo for China, India, and the shadow fleet. The Philippines is not on the guest list.

This is what a chokepoint war looks like 7,000 kilometres from the chokepoint.

GDP contraction is projected at 1.8 to 2.5 percent for Q2 2026. Inflation has spiked to 6.8 to 7.2 percent, driven by fuel transmission into transport, food, and electricity. The stock exchange has fallen 11.4 percent year to date. Remittances, 10 percent of GDP, are at risk as overseas workers face rising costs. The worst energy shock since 1973.

The viral videos show commuters walking along EDSA and Commonwealth Avenue in Manila. These are not protests. These are people who cannot afford the jeepney fare because diesel costs have doubled. The walking is not a political statement. It is an economic fact. The fuel that powered the jeepney came from a refinery that processed crude that transited Hormuz that is now a permissioned gate operated by the IRGC that charges tolls in yuan to tankers approved by a vetting process that the Philippines has no access to and no leverage over.

The Philippines did not start this war. It has no position on Iran’s nuclear programme, no opinion on zero enrichment, no seat in the Abraham Accords, no mention in any backchannel communique. But it imports 90 percent of its oil from the region where those negotiations are failing, and the failure is measured in walking commuters and a four-day workweek for a nation of 115 million.

This is the second-order cost of the Nitrogen Trap. The first order is energy prices, insurance premiums, and Hormuz tolls. The second order is the Filipino nurse who walks two hours to her hospital shift because the jeepney cannot run. The third order, arriving in April, is the rice farmer who cannot afford the diesel to pump irrigation water because the fertiliser that fed the soil came from natural gas that transited a strait that is now a toll booth collecting yuan.

The molecules are trapped at the source. The consequences arrive at the periphery. The Philippines is the canary. It will not be the last.

Thirty-nine days of jet fuel. Forty-six days of diesel. Fifty-three days of gasoline. The countdown runs whether or not the pause expires Saturday, whether or not the 15-point plan finds a taker, whether or not MBS calls Trump again. The molecules do not know where Manila is. They know they cannot get there.
